newsitem.title: BELGIUM: British beef off EU farm ministers' menu for now.
newsitem.headline: British beef off EU farm ministers' menu for now.

text.p: For the first time in many months, a worldwide ban on British beef exports will not be on the agenda at a meeting of European Union farm ministers, EU diplomats say.

But ministers will receive a progress report at the half-day meeting on Monday, their first in 1997, on proposals aimed at restoring confidence, dented by the madcow crisis, through the introduction of cattle passports and beef labels.

The EU imposed the export ban in March 1996 after the British government caused consumer panic by disclosing that madcow disease -- Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE)-- could be transmitted to humans as Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease (CJD).

"There is nothing sufficiently important now to justify raising it (the ban) at (EU Farm) Council level," said one diplomat, noting that Britain submits fortnightly progress reports to the EU's executive European Commission.

The next step in Britain's campaign to lift the ban will be British farm minister Douglas Hogg's presentation, possibly at the end of January, of a plan to exempt from the embargo herds certified to be free of the disease.
British farming officials said that the British government was still consulting the industry. About 165,000 cases of madcow disease have been reported in Britain.
"The important thing is to get it right, rather than rush it and falsely raise hopes," said one official.
Northern Irish grass-fed herds, which are tracked from birth by a computerised system, are likely to be the first to be exempted from the ban, officials said.

But they said the British proposals would first have to be examined by various EU scientific and multidisciplinary committees before being sent to the European Commission for approval and this could take several months.

Diplomats said Dutch Farm Minister, Jozias Van Aartsen, whose country took over the EU presidency on January 1, is expected to tell ministers on Monday that the proposals for cattle passports and beef labels needed more work.
"Progress has been made but details, such as whether cattle passports and a computer data base are both needed, still have to be settled," said a Dutch official.

Several member states are pressing for EU financial aid in setting up computerised systems to identify cattle and track their movements and have complained that the January 1998 deadline is too early.
Under this plan it would be compulsory for all cattle to wear ear tags and have passports and for farmers to keep up-to- date registers.
Countries are split over whether beef labelling should be voluntary or compulsory and what details -- such as birthplace, feeding and slaughtering -- should be included.
